→ Dialysis!

[Pericardial effusion]

Infiltrative

  • Malignant cells invade other organs/blood vessels
  • Happens after radiation therapy / head&neck surgery

  • Blood vessels are weak/fragile & prone to this

  • Emergent treatment!

  • Control the bleeding

  • Take w/ food
  • Monitor
  • Renal function

  • Less GI irritation (still bleeding risk)

*Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration to reduce GI, renal, & cardiovascular adverse effects*

NSAIDs

  • Affect COX1 & COX2

  • Report/monitor

  • Inquire about OTC meds!

Degenerative Joint Disease

  • NOT a normal part of aging!

Patho

Healthy Cartilage

  • Smooth, lubricated joint surface

Cartilage Breakdown

  • Progressive breakdown & wear → Where osteoarthritis begins!

Joint Changes

  • Formation of osteophytes (bone spurs)

Musculoskeletal Effects

  • Limited ROM & pain

Joints

  • Affects weight bearing joints
  • Hips, knees
  • Pain w/ activity
  • Improves w/ rest in early stages!
  • Late = Pain can happen even during rest/at night
  • Sleep disturbances
  • Osteoarthritis of the hip
  • Pain that radiates to → buttock, groin, thighs, knees
  • Joint stiffness
  • After prolonged periods of sitting/inactivity
  • Morning stiffness ( < 30 min)
  • Excess activity can increase swelling at joints
  • Crepitus
  • Grading/cracking/grinding sound when they move their joints
  • Usually asymmetric!
  • Decreased ROM

Deformities

  • Herberden nodes (DIP)
  • Distal interphalangeal joints
  • END of the fingertip
  • Bouchard nodes (PIP)
  • Proximal interphalangeal joints
  • Middle finger joint
  • [Both of these will be enlarged, swollen, red, tender]
  • Osteoarthritis of the knees
  • Bow-legged (Genu Varum)
  • Knock-kneed (Genu Valgum)

Diagnostics / Labs

X-ray

  • Joint space narrowing (as cartilage disappears)

[No blood test can confirm osteoarthritis]

Pharm

Disease-Modifying Osteoarthritis Drugs (DMOARDs)

  • [These are still being studied to see if they can slow down joint damage or support cartilage itself]

Eucalyptus oil, Menthol, Camphor creams

  • Reduce discomfort [warm/cool sensation]

Salicylate Creams / Aspercreme - Topical

  • Provide temporary relief to location it’s applied

Diclofenac Gel

  • Topical NSAID!

NSAIDs

  • naproxen (Aleve)
  • non-selective
  • ibuprofen (Advil)
  • non-selective
  • celecoxib (Celebrex)
  • Selective COX-2 inhibitor

NSAID safety

  • Avoid combining topical & oral NSAIDs
  • Monitor GI bleeding & renal effects

Nursing / Teaching

  • Balance activity & rest
  • Braces/splints/walkers
  • Heat = reduces stiffness
  • Cold = reduces pain/swelling

Patho

Stage 1

  • Autoimmune Synovial Inflammation
  • Immune complexes form
  • Synovial inflammation
  • Cytokine release

Stage 2

  • Pannus Formation
  • Synovial membrane thickens
  • Granulation tissue develops
  • Cartilage invasion

Stage 3

  • Cartilage & Bone Destruction
  • Enzyme release
  • Cartilage erosion
  • Fibrous ankylosis (stiffening of the joint, limiting ROM)

Stage 4

  • Joint Deformity
  • Bony ankylosis
  • Joint fusion
  • Permanent disability

S&S

  • Pain increased w/ movement
  • Improve somewhat w/ rest
  • Morning stiffness lasting MORE than 1 hr

Joints

Symmetrical

  • MCP (metacarpophalangeal) = knuckle
  • PIP (proximal interphalangeal) = middle joints of all fingers
  • MTP (metatarsal phalanges) = joint where the toes meet the foot
  • Hand joints “spindle”
  • D/t synovial hypertrophy & thickening of joint

Subluxation

  • 1 bone partially slips out of normal position

Ulnar drift [Knuckes]

  • Fingers deviate TOWARD the middle finger

Hallux Valgus =

  • Big toe leans toward the 2nd toe - causes painful bony bump on inner side of foot

Boutonnière

  • Distal joint is hyperextended
  • PIP joint = flexed (middle joints of fingers)

Swan-Neck Deformity

  • Hyperextension of the PIP (middle joints of fingers)
  • Flexion of the DIP (distal fingertip joint)

Extra-articular (Systemic) S&S:

  • Fever, fatigue, weight loss
  • Rheumatoid nodules
  • Firm, nontender bumps over pressure points (ex: elbows)
  • Sjögren syndrome
  • Damages lacrimal/salivary ducts (dry eyes/mouth)
  • Atherosclerosis
  • Increases chance of heart attack/stroke
  • [d/t chronic inflammation damaging endothelial lining of blood vessels]
  • Felty syndrome
  • Rare, causes enlarged spleen & low WBC count
  • Risk for infection
  • ↑ CRP
  • C-reactive protein: Inflammatory marker
  • High level = high degree of inflammation

Diagnostics

Blood tests

  • Rheumatoid Factor (RF)
  • Doesn’t guarantee diagnosis
  • Negative doesn’t mean they don’t have it
  • Anti-CCP Antibodies
  • Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide = antibodies that are more specific to RA than RF
  • If BOTH Anti-CCP & RF are present + symptoms = diagnosis is strongly supported
  • ANA, ESR, & CRP
  • ANA = AntiNuclear Antibodies (indicate autoimmune activity)
  • ESR = Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate
  • CRP = C Reactive Protein
  • (ESR & CRP = inflammatory markers & indicate how active the dz is & if it’s responding to treatment)

Synovial Fluid Analysis

  • Cloudy, straw-colored fluid
  • ↑ WBCs
  • [because it’s an active cellular war zone]
  • Flecks of fibrin
  • ↑ MMP-3
  • Matrix metalloproteinase-3 = enzyme that contributes to cartilage destruction

Surgery

  • Synovectomy
  • Removes inflamed synovial lining of joint
  • Arthroplasty for advanced disease
  • Replace the damaged joint w/ artificial joint

Pharmacology

DMARDS:

Methotrexate (Rheumatrex)

  • 1st line for RA

Purpose

  • Slows RA progression
  • Prevents joint erosion & deformity
  • Does not provide immediate pain relief

Monitor

  • Bone marrow suppression
  • Increased infection risk
  • Monitor CBC
  • Liver toxicity
  • Avoid etoh!
  • Report severe fatigue, R abdominal pain
  • Renal function

Patient teaching

  • Taken once weekly, not daily
  • [Daily use is toxic & can be fatal]
  • NO live vaccines!

SE:

  • GI discomfort
  • Mouth sores
  • Treat w/ → Folic acid
  • Avoid pregnancy
  • R/O pregnancy BEFORE starting med!
  • Avoid alcohol
  • Report
  • Signs of infection
  • SOB
  • Nausea
  • Persistent mouth sores
  • Fever
  • Bleeding

Biologic Response Modifiers…..

RESUME HERE

Severe bone infection

  • Involves bone, bone marrow, & sometimes surrounding tissue
  • Staphylococcus aureus = main bacteria

Etiology

Hematogenous Spread

  • Blood-borne spread from infection elsewhere in the body [indirect route]

Direct Inoculation

  • D/t Trauma, surgery, open fractures, around prosthetic joint → bone

Contiguous Spread

  • From adjacent infected soft tissue, infected joint, diabetic foot ulcer, pressure injury

Patho

  1. Infection & pressure
  • Bacteria invade bone
  • Inflammation & pressure ↑
  1. Bone Ischemia & Necrosis
  • Compressed blood vessels
  • ↓ bone blood flow
  1. Sequestrum Formation
  • Dead bone separates from living bone
  • Poor immune & antibiotic response
  1. Chronic Infection
  • Sequestrum reservoir
  • Persistent infection
  • Sinus tract & drainage form

[Antibiotic can’t reach the infection once the sequestrum forms]

S&S

Acute

  • Duration
  • < 1 month
  • Pain
  • Pain worsens w/ activity & is NOT relieved by rest
  • Local
  • Swelling, warmth, tenderness, ↓ ROM [d/t pain/inflammation]
  • Systemic
  • Fever, chills, night sweats, malaise
  • Restlessness, nausea, fatigue
  • Wound
  • Late: drainage may develop

Chronic

  • Duration
  • > 1 month, persistent, recurrent
  • Pain
  • Persistent localized bone pain
  • Local
  • Tissue changes → granulation tissue gets replaced by → scar tissue
  • Scar tissue = poor blood supply & makes it hard for antibiotics to get to the infection
  • Wound
  • Sinus tract & recurrent drainage

Diagnostics

Labs

  • ↑ WBC
  • ↑ ESR
  • ↑ CRP
  • Biopsy of bone/deep soft tissue

MRI

  • Detect bone marrow edema & how nearby tissues are involved

Pharmacology

Vancomycin

  • MRSA coverage
  • Monitor peak/trough levels
  • Trough = med is effectively killing the bacteria
  • Peak = to ensure they’re getting therapeutic levels & not toxic
  • Nephrotoxicity
  • Monitor BUN, creatinine
  • Administer SLOW into IV
  • Fast administration causes Red Man Syndrome
  • Pt will take it for 4-6 weeks, can be discharged w/ PICC line & self administer the med

Aminoglycosides

  • Gentamycin & Tobramycin
  • Gram-negative coverage
  • Monitor peak / trough levels
  • Ototoxicity & nephrotoxicity
  • Oto = ringing in the ears, hearing changes, balance problems, dizziness,
  • Nephro = reduced UOP

*High dose antibiotics, esp vanco/aminoglycosides can increase Pt’s risk for

  • C.Diff, oral thrush / fungal infections
  • [monitor for secondary super infections!]

Fluoroquinolones

  • Ciprofloxacin
  • Good bone penetration
  • Oral step-down therapy
  • Tendon rupture / tendonitis
  • If Pt likes to exercise = Pt needs to take it easy or stop exercising if tendons are getting sore
  • Take med w/ lots of water
  • Do NOT take w/ calcium, iron, mag, antacids [reduces absorption]
  • Photosensitivity

Nursing

  • Long IV antibiotic therapy
  • Provide support, this is a chronic condition!

Pain

  • Analgesics
  • NSAIDs, opioids
  • Muscle relaxants
  • Splints
  • To reduce pain & immobilize infected bone

Infection control

  • Sterile wound care

Monitor therapy

  • Peak / trough levels
  • Toxicity

Education

  • Recurrence
  • Home antibiotics
  • How to do a sterile dressing change
  • Wound care

Mobility

  • Repositioning
  • Splint / boot
  • PT / OT

*Someone w/ osteomyelitis, esp in lower extremities

→ Support foot in neutral position, wear boot, otherwise they can develop

→ Foot drop [contracture of Achille’s Tendon]

  • [Foot is stuck pointing down & can permanently alter their gait!

• Tiny structural problem in inner ear
  • Inside inner ear, fluid overproduces/fails to drain → creates intense build up of pressure

→ Pressure =

Gradual sensorineural hearing loss

Tinnitus

Episodic vertigo

  • “Drop attacks” → Pressure gets so intense that the brain receives a screaming signal that the body is being whirled to the floor
  • → Pt physically collapses
  • [Brain is trying to compensate for a fall that isn’t actually happening]
  • Administer CNS depressant [antihistamine, anticholinergic, benzodiazepines]
  • Fall precautions!
  • Low stimulation [dark, quiet room, stimulation can worsen vertigo]

Diagnostics

  • Glycerol test
  • → [sugar alcohol drink] → osmotic diuretic that increases osmotic pressure in blood stream → pulling fluid out of ears [& body]
  • Perform serial audiograms [hearing test]
  • Hearing & speech improves? → Diagnosis of Meniere’s Disease

Nursing

  • Daily diuretics

Teach

  • NO swimming underwater, ladders/elevated platforms

Acute confusion that develops over hours → days

Patho

  • Multi system failure d/t
  • Impaired cerebral oxygen metabolism
  • → neurons suddenly cannot extract/utilize oxygen effectively
  • → total neurotransmitter chaos
  • ↓ Acetylcholine plummets
  • ↑ Dopamine spikes
  • Brain’s ability to filter information shatters

There’s a lot of potential, reversible causes:

D - Dementia, dehydration

E - Electrolyte imbalances, emotional stress

L - Lung, liver, heart, kidney, brain

I - Infection, intensive care unit (ICU)

R - Rx drugs

I - Injury, immobility

U - Untreated pain, unfamiliar environment

M - Metabolic disorders

S&S

Hallmark = Impaired attention

  • Impaired speech
  • Rapid, rambling, disorganized, incoherent

↑ Hyperactive

  • Pts are visibly distressed

↓ Hypoactive

  • Pt’s seem sleepy rather than confused

↕ Mixed

  • Alternate between hyperactive & hypoactive
  • Loss of appetite
  • Disorganized thinking
  • As it progresses → misperceptions, misinterpretations, hallucinations

Diagnostics

CAM Tool- Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) scoring

2 things need to be present:

  • [Acute fluctuating onset
  • Severe inattention]

Pharmacology

*Meds ONLY if Pt is SEVERELY AGITATED!*

Haloperidol

  • Antipsychotic

SE:

  • Significant sedation
  • Hypotension
  • Falls
  • Extrapyramidal SE
  • (involuntary motor issues d/t the med blocking dopamine pathways)
  • QT interval prolongation
  • (get baseline EKG before starting this med)

dexmedotomidine (Precedex)

  • Use in Pt’s who are on ventilators & agitated/delirious
  • Interfering w/ wean/extubating the Pt

Monitor

  • Bradycardia
  • Hypotension

Benzodiazepines

  • Be careful w/ these! They may worsen confusion/sedation in a delirious patient
  • [Not generally used for routine delirium management]
  • Can be used if Pt is delirious d/t withdrawing for etoh/benzodiazepines

Patho

Neuronal damage → Synaptic dysfunction → Cognitive decline

Damage to neurons & brain pathways disrupt communication, leading to progressive cognitive & functional decline

Etiology

  • Most types are permanent & get worse over time
  • Memory loss & confusion may improve if there’s a treatable/reversible cause

REVERSIBLE Causes

  • Severe depression
  • Heavy etoh use
  • Normal pressure hydrocephalus
  • → This improves w/ a shunt
  • Infection
  • Meningitis, encephalitis, UTI
  • Head injury
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency
  • Medication side effects / drug toxicity
  • Metabolic disorders
  • Hypothyroidism can mimic dementia

cards.answerHtml:
Chronic, progressive, IRREVERSIBLE neurodegenerative disorder

Patho

  • Beta Amyloid Plaque trigger → inflammation & disrupt communication → spread to areas of the brain → affects cognitive function
  • Abnormal Tau proteins → causes Neurofibral Tangles
  • Tangles = disrupt intracellular transport & cause → neuron to die!
  • Dead neurons → cortical atrophy (brain shrinks)

S&S

Mild =

  • Loss of recent memories

Moderate =

  • Loss of remote/long & recent

Retrogenesis

  • Functional decline in reverse order of normal childhood development
  • Mild
  • Ages 8-12
  • Difficulty w/ complex tasks
  • Finances, meds, planning, driving
  • Basic self-care mostly preserved
  • Moderate
  • Ages 2-7
  • Needs help w/ daily activities
  • Dressing, bathing, hygiene, ADLs,
  • Benefits from simple, familiar activities
  • Simple puzzles, sorting, music, familiar household tasks provide enjoyment & sense of success
  • Severe
  • ~1 year
  • Total dependence
  • Limited communication/mobility

Nursing application for Retrogenesis

  • Do NOT to treat the adult patient like a child
  • Maintain dignity, respect, & adult identity

Diagnosis

[table at the end]

  • ONLY definitive diagnosis = brain autopsy at DEATH [plaques/tangles]
  • MMSE - Baseline screening
  • MoCa - (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) Clock drawing test
  • PET scan
  • Brain metabolism
  • Amyloid deposition
  • CT / MRI
  • Cortical atrophy
  • CSF Biomarkers
  • ↓ 𝛃-amyloid, ↑ tau proteins
  • Genetic testing
  • APOE-Ɛ4, PSEN₁/₂ (selected cases)

Pharmacology

Cholinesterase Inhibitors

donepezil (Aricept)

Mechanism

  • ↑ Acetylcholine by inhibiting cholinesterase
  • Prevent acetylcholine breakdown to allow acetylcholine to carry messages between neurons for a much longer time

Side effects

[More acetylcholine stimulates the GI tract → N/V/etc]

  • N / V
  • Diarrhea
  • Loss of appetite
  • Weight loss

[Anticholinergic effects slow down the heart rate]

  • Bradycardia
  • Dizziness
  • Syncope

Monitor

  • Pulse
  • Weight
  • Hydration status

Implement fall precautions!

Rivastigmine

Galantamine

  • Used for mild to moderate Alzheimer’s

N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) antagonist:

memantine (Namenda)

Mechanism

  • Blocks the action of glutamate

Monitor

  • Increased fall risk!
  • Esp. when first starting this med
  • Renal function

*May be used in combination w/ a cholinesterase inhibitor*

Treating depression can improve mood & can improve their cognitive functioning!

Antidepressants:

1st Line =

  • SSRIs:
  • fluoxetine
  • sertraline
  • citalopram
  • Additional options:
  • Trazodone

Indication

  • Depression & anxiety
